item.title: What "Theo of Golden" Teaches Us About Mattering
item.description:
Relationships

What "Theo of Golden" Teaches Us About Mattering

Noticing, showing care, and contributing are how people learn that they matter.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Mattering involves both feeling valued and knowing that we add value to others.
  • Noticing something and following up on it can communicate that a person matters to us.
  • We become mattering agents by helping others feel seen, cared about, and able to contribute.

There are no spoilers below.

I recently finished Allen Levi's novel Theo of Golden, and I loved it. I have since been reflecting on it, on its characters, and on what Theo is doing with the people around him.

The engine of the story is Theo's project to buy portraits of the residents of Golden and return them to the people they depict, asking only for that person's story in exchange. What stayed with me was the sheer amount of attention Theo gives to ordinary people who do not seem used to receiving any. He notices them, gets curious, asks about their lives, and then he remembers, and finds ways to let them know that what they told him stuck.

Isaac Prilleltensky has described mattering as two experiences that have to occur together: feeling valued and adding value. We need to be acknowledged and appreciated by others, and to feel that we contribute something to their lives. Have one without the other, and something still feels off.

Theo's encounters supply both.

It starts with attention

Attention has been at the center of the research on mattering from the beginning. When Morris Rosenberg and B. Claire McCullough first described it, they framed it in terms of whether other people depend on us, regard us as important, and pay attention to us. Of those, they suspected attention was the most basic—the ingredient on which the others rest.

Most of us know this feeling from the receiving end. A friend brings up something we mentioned weeks ago. A colleague notices that we have been quiet lately. Someone asks how our appointment went or asks a second question instead of nodding and changing the subject. The underlying message is important: You stayed with me.

Theo does this over and over again. He meets people, becomes interested in them, and gives them something most of us are short on: unhurried time.

Gordon Flett and Taryn Nepon have suggested that feeling cared about is a central part of mattering, and that what reaches us is how other people show that they care about us in ways we can actually detect.

Theo does something with what he notices. He gives people his time, follows through on what he said he would do, and his concern becomes something the other person can feel.

This raises an uncomfortable question for readers: We may care a great deal about the people in our lives, but do they know?

Why you can feel lonely in a room full of friends

Mattering is more than belonging. You can be a longtime member of a group, invited to every gathering, included on all the chats, and still suspect that nothing much would change if you stopped showing up. Belonging is about membership; mattering is about consequence.

Research on loneliness associates feelings of insignificance and invisibility with greater loneliness, which suggests the core issue is not the size of a person's social world, but their belief about their place in it.

There is a second half to Theo's story that can be easy to miss. He both helps others feel valued and adds value to their lives. Prilleltensky's point is that we need both. We want evidence that our lives have worth and that we have made a difference in someone else's life. Theo's project gives him a steady supply of the second, which may be part of why a man who lives so quietly seems so at home in what he is doing.

Prilleltensky has described people who foster mattering in others as mattering agents. Theo is a wonderful example of someone who actively creates experiences of mattering for other people.

Becoming a mattering agent

Few of us are going to take on a project like Theo's, but we don't need to; most mattering is communicated in unremarkable moments:

  • Notice. Being noticed is often the first evidence anyone has that they matter. You can make sure to notice the colleague who has gone quiet, or whose contribution was ignored, or the friend who seems slightly off.
  • Ask the second question. "How are you?" is a greeting. The follow-up is a conversation. Circling back to something someone told you last month tells them that their words did not evaporate the moment they walked away.
  • Say it out loud. Do not assume people know what they mean to you. Send the message. Mark the date. Name the specific thing you appreciate rather than the general one.
  • Tell people when they have made a difference. This is the half we forget. If something a person did helped you, changed how you were thinking, or made your week easier, they may have no idea unless you tell them.
  • Give people something to contribute. Ask for an opinion you actually want, or accept the offer of help. Making room for what someone is good at can say "you matter here" even more convincingly than a compliment.

Theo is generous and good with people, but what stayed with me was how he pays close enough attention so that the person across from him walks away knowing they were seen. That is available to most of us, most days, for the price of slowing down.

item.title: Why a Moment Can Matter Even When We Don't Remember It
item.description:
Memory

Why a Moment Can Matter Even When We Don't Remember It

Feelings can persist even when we can no longer remember the facts that caused them.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Remembering an experience and being emotionally affected by it are not the same thing.
  • Feelings can persist after the event that caused them has been forgotten.
  • Meaningful interactions matter even when they cannot later be recalled.
  • This has important implications for how we care for people living with dementia.
Source: MAFPHOTOART8 / Shutterstock

Imagine spending an afternoon with someone you dearly love. You sit outside in the sun, share some laughs, listen to yacht rock hits from the ’70s and sing all the lyrics with the kind of shared joy that can only emerge between the two of you. Maybe you share a latte and a piece of caramel cake.

An hour later, they have no explicit memory that you were there.

For families living with Alzheimer’s disease and other causes of significant brain change, experiences like this can be heartbreaking. When someone repeatedly forgets our visits, our conversations, and the things we have done together, it’s natural to wonder: Did it even matter?

As a caregiver turned board-certified neuropsychologist, I think science offers a reassuring answer.

Memory Is Not One Thing

We tend to think about memory as though it were a solitary ability: You either remember something or you don’t. The brain is much more complex than that.

Remembering how to cook a meatloaf, knowing how to ride a skateboard, recognizing your favorite love song, and experiencing the emotional effects of an encounter rely on overlapping but distinguishable brain systems.

Alzheimer’s disease, one of the most common causes of dementia, does not affect every part of the brain equally or at the same time. Early in the disease, there is often significant disruption of medial temporal brain systems, including the hippocampus, that are critical for forming and retaining new declarative memories: the conscious record of what happened, where it happened, and when. But those are not the only ways our brains register experience. Other neural systems contribute to emotion, familiarity, habits, reward, movement, and our responses to other people. These abilities can follow different trajectories as the disease progresses.

This helps explain something families often find puzzling: Someone may genuinely enjoy a visit from her sister but, a short time later, be unable to remember that the visit occurred. It is tempting to assume that if the memory is gone, the experience is gone too. Research suggests otherwise.

Source: dan quiet life/ Shutterstock

When Feelings Outlast Facts

One of the most compelling demonstrations came from neuropsychological research at the University of Iowa. In 2010, Feinstein and colleagues studied people with severe amnesia following damage to both hippocampi. Participants watched films designed to evoke happiness or sadness. Although they soon lost conscious memory of what they had watched, the emotions produced by the films persisted (Feinstein, Duff, & Tranel, 2010).

Researchers later asked whether the same phenomenon would occur in Alzheimer’s disease. In 2014, Guzmán-Vélez and colleagues studied 17 people with probable Alzheimer’s disease and 17 healthy comparison participants. Those with Alzheimer’s had substantial difficulty remembering the films they had watched, yet their feelings persisted beyond their memories for them. Some continued to experience sadness for more than 30 minutes despite having no conscious recollection of what had caused it (Guzmán-Vélez, Feinstein, & Tranel, 2014).

More recent science strengthens this insight. A 2025 systematic review in Nature Mental Health examined 35 studies of emotional memory in Alzheimer’s disease and found evidence that emotion can continue to influence memory even in the presence of significant cognitive change. Across the studies, emotionally meaningful information was sometimes remembered better than neutral information, with the effect influenced by factors such as emotional intensity, the type of experience, and how information was encoded. Neuroimaging findings pointed to the amygdala and hippocampus as important contributors to these effects (Kapoor, Mather, & Nation, 2025).

This does not mean that emotion, or emotional memory, is untouched by Alzheimer’s disease. It means something far more useful: Memory loss does not make a person emotionally unreachable. An experience can still register, impact how someone feels, and sometimes even strengthen what is retained when the details of the experience itself become difficult to retrieve. Remembering an experience and being affected by it are not the same thing.

Rethinking “He Won’t Remember”

In my work with families, I often hear some version of: Why take Dad out? He won’t remember it tomorrow. Or, I visited Mom yesterday, but today she doesn’t even remember I was there. Sometimes I hear the more painful version: I stopped visiting when she couldn’t remember who I was anymore.

The memory loss may be very real. What deserves reconsideration is the assumption underneath it: If an experience cannot later be remembered, is it less meaningful?

A person may forget the delicious BLT but still have experienced pleasure while eating it. She may forget the visitor but still have spent an hour feeling safe and loved and sleep better that night. He may forget the music but still have tapped his foot, smiled, sung along, and experienced genuine connection.

The opposite deserves our attention, too: An upsetting interaction does not necessarily become harmless because someone cannot later describe what happened. The conscious narrative may fade while some of its emotional effects linger.

These are some of the reasons the environment surrounding a person with dementia matters so much. Agitation, withdrawal, or distress should not automatically be understood only as symptoms arising from a diseased brain. Pain, overstimulation, loneliness, communication demands, fear, and the way other people approach and respond to someone can all influence behavior.

A Different Way to Measure a Good Day

Memory can easily become our primary scorecard. We ask whether someone remembered the outing, our name, or that we visited. Instead, we can also pay attention to what happened while we were together.

Did she laugh? Did he feel included? Was there music he enjoyed, a hand to hold, something interesting to see, or someone who looked him in the eye and seemed genuinely glad he was there? Did this person experience pleasure, safety, connection, or belonging? Those experiences don’t have to become permanent autobiographical memories before they are allowed to count.

A good hour is still a good hour, even if someone cannot tell us about it tomorrow.

What This Science Asks of Us

If someone you love is living with brain change, shift the goal from creating an experience they will remember tomorrow to creating an experience that feels good today.

Take the drive. Play the favorite song for the hundredth time. Sit outside together. Share something delicious. Offer your full attention. Instead of asking Will they remember this? ask How are they experiencing this right now?

Pay attention to what the person shows you: a smile, relaxed shoulders, laughter, singing, reaching for your hand, lingering at the table, or simply becoming more settled. And remember that distress may linger, too. Being rushed, repeatedly corrected, embarrassed, frightened, or spoken about as though they aren’t there may leave an emotional impact even when the details are later forgotten.

Perhaps the most practical lesson is also the simplest: Don’t make remembering the price of admission for having a meaningful life.

Source: KDS Productions

What Changing Brains Can Teach Us

Like many things I have learned about dementia in my career, this research reaches beyond neurodegenerative disease and tells us something about being human.

Think about the experiences that shaped you but that you can no longer consciously retrieve: a teacher’s genuine smile at a job well done, a parent’s tenderness when you weren’t your best self, the feeling of being welcomed into a new group of friends, or hundreds of ordinary moments of connection that make a life beautiful.

Most are no longer available to us as discrete memories. Yet it would be strange to conclude that they had no effect on who we became.

Perhaps this is one thing changing brains can reveal about being human: We sometimes confuse remembering an experience with having been changed by it.

A moment does not have to be remembered forever to matter.

item.title: Embracing an Animal's Perspective Can Be a Life-Changer
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Embracing an Animal's Perspective Can Be a Life-Changer

Risë VanFleet's book is a must read for anyone living with a companion animal.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • A paradigm-changing book for improving all human-animal relationships.
  • Forming reciprocal, two-way consenting relationships should be everyone's goal.
Source: Michal Petráš/Pexels

Just about everyone who chooses to live with a companion animal (AKA "pet") wants their nonhuman friend to have the best life possible. While there are some exceptions, I can only hope that these people, along with those who already are dedicated to giving their nonhuman friends the best lives possible, will read, reread, and share Dr. Risë VanFleet's book titled Embracing the Animal's Perspective: Living Our Best Lives With Companion Animals.

In this remarkable science- and story-based interdisciplinary book, VanFleet weaves in vital information from different fields including "ethology, humanistic psychology, cognitive psychology, behaviorism, comparative psychology, interpersonal theory, systems theory, bioecological systems, and development and attachment theory."

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Embracing the Animal’s Perspective?

Risë VanFleet: Sometimes, I see examples where people do not understand their animals accurately. I was there once myself. A wonderful eye-opener for me came long ago, when I began to see my own animals more clearly. In my workshops for therapists learning animal-assisted play therapy, we have emphasized how understanding animals’ perspectives benefits people and animals alike. Participants have been very positive about this; the book is a way to share these ideas with more people.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

RV: I have many interests, and this book highlights some key ones. I’m a relationship-focused family psychologist, and I also love animals. I have studied ethology and animal behavior for years. Your work, Marc, has been very influential in my journey. I find our human-animal relationships fascinating, and I want everyone to enjoy them in respectful ways that see each person and each animal as an individual.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

RV: After working with professionals who work with animals, I saw how things I taught helped them. Many described their increased awareness of animals as “life-changing,” and I wanted to share that experience for anyone who lives with and loves animals, and even for those who sometimes become frustrated with their companion animals. This is the first book I’ve written for the public at large (others were for human or animal professionals), and I’ve included real-life examples for dogs, horses, and cats; the material applies to other species, too. I wanted to share some core skills and ideas that help people see their animals more clearly. That leads to better relationships and mutual enjoyment of life together. This book might be useful for those who enjoy their companion animals as well as animal professionals and therapists.

Source: Risë VanFleet.

MB: What topics do you consider, and what are some of your major messages?

RV: This is not a book about training animals—there are many of them available. I focus more on building relationships based on understanding our animals better. In a way, it’s about learning by listening to the animals themselves. The book is divided into sections, each with several chapters. Each section includes science-based concepts along with many practical examples. I've included parallels among species, as well as with wild animals.

Expectations: How we can develop realistic expectations of our animals based on observations, understanding their natural behaviors, and getting to know them as unique individuals.

Empathy: How we can see and accept each animal’s perspective to build relationships responsive to their needs while determining their best fit for the activities we ask them to do.

Exploration: When we understand the need to explore and search the environments in which our animals (and we) live, we can increase their motivation, solve problems that occur, and share enjoyable adventures.

Empowerment: We explore ways to give our animals greater agency when possible and practical—allowing them to make more choices that affect and enrich their lives. We consider the role of control along with comparisons of wild animals and our domesticated companion animals. This section highlights the positive impact of obtaining animal consent and input more frequently, reducing our intrusiveness, and linking empowerment to animal welfare and our own well-being and connections.

Enthusiasm: How we can increase the enjoyment and fun in our relationships with animals, the value of play for animals and their people, and how we can understand animals’ social relationships with other animals and with us.

The book prompts readers to consider how well their lifestyles serve their animals and themselves, and how small changes can make big, positive differences.

MB: How does your book differ from others that consider some of the same general topics?

RVF: While I have blended the practical with the scientific and drawn from many aspects of my own experiences, this book was in reality created by the many animals I have known. This includes my lifetime with companion animals, the countless dogs in rescue environments with whom I volunteered for 25 years, the animals who inspired the way we teach animal-assisted play therapy in an animal-centered way, and the many with whom I’ve conducted behavioral consults to help animals and their humans live more compatibly in their homes. All of them had something to say, and the better I listened, the better things turned out. As far as I know, it’s the first of its kind to combine these specific elements and show how they work together; a better understanding of companion animals will also increase our confidence and satisfaction with our relationships with animals in our lives. There are, of course, many wonderful books available (including your own), and I’ve referenced many of them in my book for readers to dive into topics. Perhaps of most use is the ability to read this book and try its ideas with one’s own animal friends.

MB: Will learning to see through a pet's eyes improve how we live with them?

RV: Absolutely. The reader can easily try the ideas in the book, and the more we understand our animals, the less frustration we feel and the more our animals enjoy being with us. I hope readers will see that when we regularly look for, pay attention to, and respond to each animal’s perspective, it allows our animals to be who they are while also enriching our own lives.
